objectives.label: Distance between two points
objectives.description: Calculate the distance between two points on the coordinate plane using the distance rule (including points on an axis and the distance from the origin).

objectives.label: Prove shapes using distances
objectives.description: Use side and diagonal lengths found with the distance rule to prove that four points are the vertices of a parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus or square, or that a triangle is right angled (converse of the Pythagorean theorem), and calculate its area.

objectives.label: Collinear points and circle
objectives.description: Use distances to show that three points are collinear (the sum of two distances equals the third) or that points lie on a circle with a given center (equal distances).

entries.text: The two points A(3, 0), B(-1, 0) are both located on the x-axis, so AB = |-1 - 3| = |-4|, so AB = 4 unit length. $AB=|-1-3|=|-4|=4$

A.why: Distance between points on the x-axis uses the absolute difference.

B.why: Distance between two points on the x-axis.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with X and Y axes; point B(-1, 0) and point A(3, 0) marked on the x-axis; axis ticks -2, -1, 1, 2, 3 on x and 1, 2, 3, -1, -2 on y.

A.why: Shows A and B on the x-axis for the distance example.

B.why: Shows A and B on the x-axis for the axis distance.

entries.text: The two points C(0, -3), D(0, -1) are both located in the y-axis, so CD = |-3 - (-1)| = |-3 + 1| = |-2|, CD = 2 unit length. $CD=|-3-(-1)|=|-3+1|=|-2|=2$

A.why: Distance between points on the y-axis uses the absolute difference.

B.why: Distance between two points on the y-axis.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with X and Y axes; point D(0, -1) and point C(0, -3) marked on the y-axis; ticks -2, -1, 1, 2 on x and -1, -2, -3 on y; point labels read from figure.

A.why: Shows C and D on the y-axis for the distance example.

B.why: Shows C and D on the y-axis for the axis distance.

entries.text: The points M(3, 2), N(7, 5) are represented graphically in the figure. To find the length of MN: MK = |7 - 3| = 4 unit length, NK = |5 - 2| = 3 unit length. Triangle MKN is right angled at K, therefore (MN)^2 = (MK)^2 + (KN)^2 (Pythagoren theory), (MN)^2 = (3)^2 + (4)^2, (LM)^2 = 9 + 16, (MN)^2 = 25, therefore MN = 5 unit length. $(MN)^2=(MK)^2+(KN)^2=3^2+4^2=25,\ MN=5$

A.why: Finds MN using the Pythagorean theorem on the coordinate plane.

B.why: Works out the distance MN using a right triangle.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with X and Y axes, x ticks 1–8, y ticks 1–7. Points M and N joined by a segment, labelled M (2, 3) and N (5, 7) (coordinates printed reversed relative to text M(3,2), N(7,5)); K at the corner of the right triangle below N and right of M; leg labels '3 - 7' along MK and '2 - 5' along NK; dashed lines.

A.why: Shows the right triangle MKN used to find distance MN.

B.why: Figure for finding MN with M(3,2), N(7,5) by the Pythagorean theorem.

entries.text: Coordinate plane with axes x'x and y'y, origin O. Right triangle MKN (right angle at K, shaded light blue) with M(x1, y1), N(x2, y2), K below N and right of M. MK labelled x2 − x1, KN labelled y2 − y1. Dotted lines from M and K down to the x-axis at points A and B.

A.why: Right triangle with general coordinates that gives the distance rule.

B.why: Right triangle MKN with leg differences illustrates deriving the distance rule.

entries.text: The distance between two points = the square root of (square of the difference in the x-axis + square of the difference in the y-axis).

A.why: States the distance rule in words.

B.why: States the distance rule in words.

entries.text: The distance of a point $M(x_1,y_1)$ from the origin point $O(0,0)$ is $OM=\sqrt{x_1^2+y_1^2}$. $OM=\sqrt{x_1^2+y_1^2}$

A.why: States the distance from the origin.

B.why: States the distance of a point from the origin.

entries.text: Axes x and y with origin o. Right triangle (shaded green) with vertices at origin, point (x1, 0) on the x-axis and M(x1, y1); right angle marked at the foot on the x-axis; horizontal leg labelled x1, vertical leg labelled y1.

A.why: Right triangle that illustrates the distance from the origin.

B.why: Right triangle with legs x1, y1 illustrates the distance from the origin.

entries.text: Coordinate plane with x and y axes (x from -7 to 3 marked, y up to 9). Blue quadrilateral ABCD with labelled points D (9 ,-2), C (5 ,-7), A (4 ,2), B (0 ,-3). Labels as printed; points read from figure, verify.

A.why: Quadrilateral ABCD for proving the shape with distances.

B.why: Quadrilateral ABCD figure goes with proving the type of quadrilateral.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with triangle ABC: A (1, 4), B (-1, -2), C (2, -3). Points read from figure; verify.

A.why: Triangle ABC for proving it is right angled.

B.why: Triangle ABC figure goes with proving the triangle is right angled.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with x and y axes from about -5 to 5. Points A(4, 3), B(1, 1) and C(-5, -3) are marked, joined by a dotted red line passing through all three.

A.why: Points A, B, C on one line illustrate collinearity.

B.why: Grid showing A, B, C on one line illustrates the collinearity exercise.

lessons.title: The Two Coordinates of the midpoint segment

objectives.label: Midpoint from the figure
objectives.description: Find the two coordinates of the midpoint of a straight segment parallel to an axis, or from a drawing, given its two ends.

objectives.label: Calculate midpoint coordinates
objectives.description: Calculate the coordinates of the midpoint of a straight segment given its two ends, using M((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2), the average of the coordinates.

objectives.label: Find missing end point
objectives.description: Determine the coordinates of an end point of a segment, or the fourth vertex of a parallelogram (and the intersection of its diagonals), given the midpoint, by solving the midpoint formula for the unknown.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with x and y axes. Horizontal segment AB at y=6 with A at x=2, B at x=6, midpoint C at x=4, tick marks on each half. Dotted vertical lines drop from A, C, B to the x-axis (x=2, 4, 6).

A.why: Horizontal segment AB with midpoint C read off the grid shows finding the midpoint from a figure.

B.why: Horizontal segment's midpoint is found from the grid, a segment parallel to an axis.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with axes; x-axis labelled -4, -3, -2, -1 on the left, y-axis labelled -1 to -5 downward. Vertical segment at x=-2 with B at y=-1, C at y=-3 (midpoint), A at y=-5, tick marks on each half, dotted horizontal lines from B, C, A to the y-axis.

A.why: Vertical segment with midpoint C read from the drawing illustrates midpoint from the figure.

B.why: Vertical segment's midpoint is read from the grid, a segment parallel to an axis.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with axes; x marked 1–5, y marked 1–6. Segment from A(1, 2) to B(5, 6) with midpoint C(3, 4), tick marks on each half. Dotted lines from A, C, B to both axes.

A.why: Segment AB with midpoint C(3, 4) read from the grid leads into the midpoint, shown from the drawing.

B.why: Grid shows the midpoint C(3,4) of a slanted segment read from the drawing.

entries.text: Midpoint C of A(1, 2) and B(5, 6) is found by averaging coordinates: C((1+5)/2, (2+6)/2), i.e. C(3, 4). $C\left(\frac{1+5}{2},\frac{2+6}{2}\right)=C(3,4)$

A.why: Averaging the coordinates of A and B to get C(3, 4) is the midpoint calculation.

B.why: Midpoint C of A(1,2) and B(5,6) is found from the drawing with dotted lines, introducing the averaging idea in an activity-type example.

entries.text: Coordinate axes x'x and y'y meeting at F. Points A(x1;y1), M(x;y), B(x2;y2) on a slanted segment AB with tick marks on AM and MB. Right triangles: D below M with AD labelled x − x1, DM labelled y − y1; E below B with ME's horizontal side labelled x2 − x, BE labelled y2 − y. Triangles AMD and MBE shaded.

A.why: The triangles AMD and MBE figure derives the midpoint formula (x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2.

B.why: The triangles AMD and MBE figure derives the midpoint formula.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with x- and y-axes, x from -4 to 5, y from 4 to -5. Parallelogram ABCD drawn in red: D (x1, y1) at about (-1, 4), A (3, 2), C (0, -3) labelled 'C (0- 3)', B at about (4, -5). Blue diagonals AC and BD cross at M, about (1.5, -0.5).

A.why: Parallelogram ABCD with diagonals meeting at M illustrates finding the fourth vertex from the midpoint.

B.why: Parallelogram ABCD with diagonals meeting at M is used to find the fourth vertex D from the midpoint.

lessons.title: The slope of the straight line

objectives.label: Slope from points or angle
objectives.description: Calculate the slope of a straight line from two points, and from the positive angle it makes with the positive direction of the x-axis using m = tan E, and find the angle from a given slope with the calculator.

objectives.label: Parallel lines and slopes
objectives.description: Use equal slopes to prove that two straight lines are parallel and to find unknown coordinates for lines parallel to an axis.

objectives.label: Perpendicular lines and slopes
objectives.description: Use the product of slopes equal to -1 to prove two straight lines are perpendicular, and to find a missing slope or coordinate.

entries.text: The slope of the straight line passing through two points $(x_1, y_1)$, $(x_2, y_2)$ equals $\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.

A.why: Slope formula from two points is assumed prior knowledge, recalled before the lesson.

B.why: Slope formula from two points is used to calculate slope.

entries.text: First: coordinate grid with a line rising to the right through (3,1) and (4,2), crossing the axes below the origin; acute angle marked at the x-axis.

A.why: Line with acute angle used to relate slope to the angle with the x-axis.

B.why: Line with acute angle, slope from two points.

entries.text: Second: coordinate grid with a line falling to the right through (4,0) and (2,2); obtuse angle marked at the x-axis.

A.why: Line with obtuse angle used to relate slope to the angle with the x-axis.

B.why: Line with obtuse angle, slope from two points.

entries.text: Third: coordinate grid with a horizontal line at y = 3 through (-1,3) and (2,3).

A.why: Horizontal line case in the slope-and-angle table.

B.why: Horizontal line example for slope from two points.

entries.text: Fourth: coordinate grid with a vertical line at x = 2 through (2,-1) and (2,3).

A.why: Vertical line case in the slope-and-angle table.

B.why: Vertical line example for slope from two points.

entries.text: An angle is positive when it is formed by a counter anticlockwise rotation and it is negative when it is formed by a clockwise rotation.

A.why: Defines positive angle, needed for m = tan E.

B.why: Defines positive angle used in m = tan E.

entries.text: Circular clock-like diagram with a + sign at the top for anticlockwise rotation (labelled 'anti') and a − sign at the bottom for clockwise rotation, with arrows around the circle.

A.why: Illustrates positive and negative rotation for the angle definition.

B.why: Shows positive (anticlockwise) angle direction used for the angle with the x-axis.

entries.text: Figure number, slope, type of positive angle the line makes with the positive direction of the x-axis, and the slope of the line. The figure number, The slope $\left(\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\right)$, The type of the positive angle that the straight line makes in the positive direction to the x-coordinates, The slope of the straight line / 1, $m=\frac{2-1}{4-3}=1$, acute, Larger than zero / 2, $m=\f

A.why: Compares slope with the type of positive angle for each line.

B.why: Relates slope from two points to the type of angle and sign of slope.

entries.text: The slope of a straight line is the tangent of the positive angle which the straight line makes with the positive direction of the x axis.

A.why: States slope is the tangent of the positive angle.

B.why: Slope is tan of the positive angle with the x-axis.

entries.text: Coordinate axes x, y with two parallel lines L1 and L2 sloping upward to the right; each makes a positive angle with the positive x-axis, marked E1 (for L2) and E2 (for L1); the lines cross the axes at different places. Labels read from the figure; verify.

A.why: Two parallel lines with equal angles lead to equal slopes.

B.why: Two parallel lines with equal angles E1, E2.

entries.text: If two lines are parallel, then their slopes are equal and vice versa.

A.why: Parallel lines have equal slopes and vice versa.

B.why: Parallel lines have equal slopes and vice versa.

entries.text: If m1 = m2 then L1 is parallel to L2. $m_1 = m_2 \Rightarrow L_1 \parallel L_2$

A.why: Equal slopes imply parallel lines.

B.why: m1 = m2 implies L1 parallel L2.

entries.text: If two lines have equal slopes, then the two lines are parallel.

A.why: Equal slopes mean parallel lines.

B.why: Equal slopes mean the lines are parallel.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with x from about -4 to 6 and y from -3 to 4. Quadrilateral ABCD drawn in blue with A(2,3), B(6,2), C(-2,-2), D(-2,1) labelled. Points read from figure; verify.

A.why: Quadrilateral ABCD is used to prove sides parallel via equal slopes.

B.why: Quadrilateral ABCD used for proving parallel sides by equal slopes.

entries.text: Coordinate axes x'x and y'y with two perpendicular lines meeting at C, above the x-axis, left of the y-axis... L1 rises to the right (arrow upper right) and passes through A on the lower left, meeting the x-axis at F? labelled A near lower-left end; L2 goes from upper left (arrow near y-axis, labelled L2) down to the right through C to B on the x-axis. Angle E marked at the x-axis where L1 crosses

A.why: Two perpendicular lines with angles E and J lead to the product of slopes.

B.why: Shows two perpendicular lines with their angles.

entries.text: Table to complete: values of angle E, angle J and Tan E1 × Tan J2 , , , , , / Values of E, 20°, 40°, ....., ....., ....... / Values of J, ......., ....., 140°, 150°, ..... / Tan E1 × Tan J2, ....., ....., ....., ....., .....

A.why: Table of tan E × tan J shows the product is -1 for perpendicular lines.

B.why: Table leads to the product of tangents being -1 for perpendicular lines.

entries.text: For two perpendicular lines, Tan E1 × Tan J2 = -1, i.e. the product of their slopes is -1: m1 × m2 = -1. $m_1\times m_2=-1$

A.why: Product of slopes of perpendicular lines is -1.

B.why: Tan E1 × Tan J2 = -1 gives product of slopes -1 for perpendicular lines.

entries.text: L1 and L2 are two straight lines with slopes m1, m2, where m1, m2 belong to R*. $m_1, m_2 \in \mathbb{R}^*$

A.why: Sets the nonzero slopes m1, m2 for the perpendicularity rule that follows.

B.why: Sets up slopes m1, m2 for the perpendicular rule.

entries.text: The product of the slopes of two perpendicular straight lines is -1, and vice versa: if m1 × m2 = -1 then L1 ⊥ L2. $m_1 \times m_2 = -1 \Rightarrow L_1 \perp L_2$

A.why: Product -1 and vice versa for perpendicular lines.

B.why: Perpendicular lines have slope product -1 and vice versa.

entries.text: If the product of the slopes of two straight lines is -1, then the two lines are perpendicular.

A.why: Product of slopes -1 means lines are perpendicular.

B.why: Product of slopes -1 gives perpendicular lines.

lessons.title: The Equation of the straight line given its slope and its y - intercept

objectives.label: Slope and y-intercept from equation
objectives.description: Determine the slope and the length of the y-intercept of a straight line from its equation, by writing it in the form y = mx + b or using m = -a/b, and use them to represent the line graphically.

objectives.label: Find equation of a line
objectives.description: Find the equation of a straight line in the form y = mx + b, given its slope (found from two points, a perpendicular line, or a bisected segment's mid-point) and a point on it.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with x and y axes, origin O, x marks -4,-3,-2 and 1,2 and y marks -1,1,2,3. A straight line rising to the right passes through (-4,0) and point B(0,2) on the y-axis, with arrows at both ends.

A.why: The line with its y-intercept at B(0,2) illustrates reading the intercept and slope from a graph, as in the graphical representation examples.

B.why: The line crossing the y-axis at B(0,2) illustrates reading the y-intercept and representing the line graphically.

entries.text: Notice that: the equation of the straight line is written ax + by + c = zero, b ≠ 0. $ax + by + c = 0,\ b \neq 0$

A.why: The general form ax + by + c = 0, b ≠ 0 is the starting point for rewriting into y = mx + b to find slope and intercept.

B.why: The general form ax + by + c = 0 with b ≠ 0 is what is rewritten as y = mx + b to find slope and y-intercept.
